guidance: The registry's Recommended column is IANA's own rating, not a security audit: N can mean limited applicability and D marks a suite that should not be negotiated. This page decodes names and codes; it does not say which suites a server should offer, and it does not read live traffic or certificates.
method: A cipher suite is a two-byte value: 0x1301 is the bytes 0x13 and 0x01, which the registry prints as {0x13,0x01}, and this page splits and recombines those bytes. TLS 1.3 names follow TLS_AEAD_HASH (RFC 9846, Appendix B.4): the name carries only the AEAD and the hash used with HKDF, because key exchange and authentication moved into the handshake as the certificate and the signature scheme, so TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 names AES-128-GCM with the SHA-256 hash and nothing about certificates. Names of TLS 1.2 and earlier read TLS_<key exchange>_WITH_<bulk cipher>_<MAC> (RFC 5246, Appendix A.5), and the key-exchange token also names the authentication, so ECDHE_RSA is ephemeral ECDH authenticated by an RSA signature while DH_anon authenticates nobody; a trailing _EXPORT marks the 40-bit suites of the export era. In the AEAD suites (GCM, CCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) the trailing hash is the PRF rather than a record MAC, and the RFC 6655 CCM suites name no hash at all because it is fixed at SHA-256, which the page reports as 'not in the name' instead of inventing one. RFC 9150's integrity-only TLS_SHA256_SHA256 and TLS_SHA384_SHA384 carry a hash and no bulk cipher. 0x00FF and 0x5600 are signalling values offered beside the suites and never selected, and the GREASE values of RFC 8701 (0x0A0A, 0x1A1A and so on, two equal bytes ending in 0xA) are deliberately unassigned. The lookup table is the IANA TLS Cipher Suites registry as fetched on 2026-11-16: all 358 named entries, with the unassigned, reserved and range rows left out, and each row keeps its registry name, Recommended flag and reference. Input is one or more names or four-digit hexadecimal codes, case-insensitive and optionally prefixed 0x, up to 32 values; a list keeps the order given, costs two bytes per suite on the wire and reports the registry status of each. Unknown names and malformed codes are refused with one message rather than being guessed at, and the whole decoder runs in the browser with no network access.
